section_summary: This section combines the end of one translated installment and the complete final installment of former Japanese Minister Yamagata’s wartime diary, documenting Axis diplomatic coordination, propaganda, intelligence work, and Chile’s January 1943 rupture of relations with Japan. It also contains policy memoranda and telegrams about Allied custody, examination, disposal, and shipment of Japanese diplomatic archives and personal property, together with Momotaro Enomoto’s assessments of repatriated Japanese officials and General Onodera’s account of wartime intelligence networks. The closing pages reproduce detailed Japanese Embassy lists classifying Belgian public figures as neutral, pro-Japanese, or anti-Japanese, followed by the beginning of an inventory of propaganda and documentary films.

subfiles.title: Continuation of the translated diary of former Japanese Minister Yamagata, September 13–October 31, 1942
subfiles.from: Yamagata, former Japanese Minister to Chile
subfiles.to: Personal diary; later translated for the U.S. Embassy in Santiago
subfiles.about: Daily entries describe Japanese diplomatic activity in Chile during mounting pressure over Axis relations and communications.
subfiles.summary: Yamagata records efforts to free Miyasaki from detention in Mendoza, consultations with Japanese and Chilean contacts, and repeated coordination with the German and Italian ambassadors. Much of the diary concerns cable restrictions, trade, Chilean domestic instability, President Ríos’s cancelled U.S. visit, and preparations for a possible rupture with the Axis. The installment ends amid a cabinet crisis, Communist demonstrations, and continued political intelligence gathering.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on interpreting the MacArthur directive governing Japanese archives and official property
subfiles.from: Frederick B. Lyon, Chief, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation
subfiles.about: FC responds to SPD’s proposed revision of the October 23, 1945 MacArthur directive concerning Japanese official property and archives.
subfiles.summary: Lyon argues that Allied custody did not require the indefinite preservation of all Japanese diplomatic archives after examination. Because title was vested jointly in the Four Allied Powers, final destruction or disposal required a common Allied policy rather than unilateral U.S. treatment of the material as public records. He recommends reexamining the directive’s interpretation and disposing of valueless records by Allied agreement, while concurring with SPD on property and liquid assets.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 7000 transmitting writings and reports by Momotaro Enomoto
subfiles.from: C. I. Ravndal, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Stockholm
subfiles.about: The Stockholm Legation forwards Enomoto’s manuscript, autobiographical report, correspondence, and observations for possible use by American authorities in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ravndal describes Enomoto as a former Mainichi Shimbun correspondent who assisted Allied efforts to locate Japanese government property in Sweden. Enomoto and his wife remained in Colombo after their young daughter became ill and died during the voyage to Japan aboard the S.S. Plus Ultra. The despatch itemizes four enclosed manuscripts and letters and suggests sending photostats to the American authorities in Japan.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding Enomoto’s report on Japanese repatriates
subfiles.from: Calvin Hawley Oakes, American Consul, Colombo
subfiles.to: Herschel V. Johnson, American Minister, Stockholm
subfiles.about: Oakes forwards a copy of Enomoto’s report and notes that Enomoto is awaiting further instructions before continuing to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The OCR is badly damaged, but the letter clearly transmits Enomoto’s communication concerning personalities in the Japanese repatriation group. Oakes retains the original in Colombo and advises that transportation authorities may soon require Enomoto to resume his journey to Japan.

subfiles.title: Enomoto’s confidential report on personalities in the Japanese repatriation group
subfiles.to: Calvin H. Oakes, U.S. Consulate, Colombo, for Adolf J. Lium
subfiles.about: Enomoto assesses Japanese diplomats, military officers, and other possible collaborators encountered aboard the S.S. Plus Ultra.
subfiles.summary: Enomoto reports that many senior diplomats opposed active cooperation with the occupation, while figures such as Generals Onodera and Tateishi, Tsuchiya, Taki, and several junior officials might support democratic or intelligence cooperation. He describes personal reputations, suspected misuse of official funds, attitudes toward the emperor, and links with European and Near Eastern intelligence contacts. He also recommends the Armenian publisher Shamlian and asks that the report be treated confidentially and forwarded to Lium.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding an appendage to Enomoto’s March 10 report
subfiles.from: Calvin Hawley Oakes, American Consul, Colombo
subfiles.to: Herschel V. Johnson, American Minister, Stockholm
subfiles.about: Oakes forwards a new appendix supplied by Enomoto and sends copies to Lium in Copenhagen.
subfiles.summary: The letter refers to Oakes’s March 14 transmission and encloses an appendage that Enomoto delivered on March 30. Because Enomoto had learned that Lium was in Copenhagen, Oakes also forwarded copies directly to the American Legation there.

subfiles.title: General Onodera’s statement on Axis and European intelligence collaboration
subfiles.from: General Onodera, transmitted by Momotaro Enomoto
subfiles.about: Onodera outlines his wartime cooperation with German and other European intelligence services and identifies potentially useful anti-Soviet networks.
subfiles.summary: Onodera describes exchanges with von Heimann and Kraemer, limited cooperation with Finnish and Hungarian officers, and Japanese reliance on European rather than native Japanese agents. He evaluates Baltic, Finnish, Polish, Swedish, and Hungarian intelligence capabilities, emphasizing Polish underground access and Finnish expertise with Soviet codes. He offers to answer further questions from Lium or a designated representative.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Enomoto memoranda to the U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo
subfiles.to: United States Political Adviser to the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department forwards photostats of Colombo despatches containing memoranda prepared by Enomoto.
subfiles.summary: The brief memorandum sends Enomoto’s material to the Political Adviser as potentially useful to that office or other SCAP headquarters sections. Its enclosures are identified as photostatic copies of the Colombo despatches and their attachments.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 13,949 transmitting the fourth and final installment of Yamagata’s diary
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, U.S. Embassy, Santiago
subfiles.about: The Embassy forwards the final translated portion of former Japanese Minister Yamagata’s diary from the Japanese archives held by the Swedish Legation.
subfiles.summary: The despatch refers to an earlier April 26 transmission and identifies the enclosure as the diary’s fourth and last installment, covering November 1, 1942, through January 29, 1943. A copy of the translation was also supplied to the British Embassy.

subfiles.title: Fourth and final translated installment of Yamagata’s diary, November 1942–January 1943
subfiles.from: Yamagata, former Japanese Minister to Chile
subfiles.to: Personal diary; later translated for the U.S. Embassy in Santiago
subfiles.about: The diary records Japan’s unsuccessful campaign to prevent Chile from breaking relations and the subsequent confinement of Japanese diplomats.
subfiles.summary: Yamagata chronicles intensive lobbying of Chilean officials, coordination with German and Italian diplomats, dissemination of the Hori Announcement, payments to intermediaries, and preparations for rupture. On January 20, 1943, Chile formally broke relations: cables were cut, a rupture note was delivered, and the Japanese Legation began moving codes, funds, and propaganda material. After disputes over the protection and treatment of diplomats in Chile and Tokyo, police confined the Japanese staff and families to the Legation on January 29, where sensitive codes were burned.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 339 reporting the limited value of Japanese archives in Bogotá
subfiles.from: John C. Wiley, U.S. Embassy, Bogotá
subfiles.about: Wiley reports that inspection found little of value in the former Japanese Legation archives and discusses their proposed Colombian custody.
subfiles.summary: The archives contained only a limited quantity of material and nothing of apparent value, a judgment shared by British and Soviet representatives. Britain raised no objection to Colombia taking custody so long as the records remained intact and accessible to the Allies. Wiley adds that photographing or microfilming the material was impracticable without a competent Japanese translator.

subfiles.title: Memorandum requesting examination of Japanese-language documents from Stockholm
subfiles.from: Herbert J. Cummings, Assistant Chief, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation
subfiles.to: Major W. L. Chan, Washington Document Center
subfiles.about: Cummings asks the Washington Document Center to identify and translate selected Japanese Legation documents obtained in Stockholm.
subfiles.summary: Commander Rufus L. Taylor selected the documents as potentially useful and removed them with the Inter-Allied Committee’s consent. The Document Center is asked to list their contents and provide translations of any material containing useful political or economic intelligence.

subfiles.title: Record-copy replacement notice for telegram file 894.414/5-2846
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Communications and Records
subfiles.about: The form designates an attached white copy as the official record copy because the yellow action copy was not returned.
subfiles.summary: The sheet is an administrative records-control notice for file 894.414/5-2846. It instructs the action office to return the attached copy to Central Records for filing.

subfiles.title: Telegram authorizing shipment of former Japanese officials’ personal effects from Rome
subfiles.to: U.S. Embassy, Rome; repeated to Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department conditionally approves sending former Japanese officials’ personal effects to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Approval depended upon concurrence by the other Allied representatives and SCAP, suitable shipping arrangements, and payment from Japanese private or joint-trust funds. Qualified officials also had to certify that the shipment contained no Japanese government property, particularly diplomatic or consular archives.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 2664 proposing shipment of Japanese officials’ effects from Rome to Tokyo
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; requested repetition to Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Embassy seeks guidance on shipping stored personal effects to Tokyo for Allied inspection and delivery to their Japanese owners.
subfiles.summary: The proposal would help empty the former Japanese Embassy building in Rome and avoid opening the effects locally, where adequate personnel and inspection facilities were unavailable. The effects would instead be inspected by Allied authorities at the Japanese port of entry before being forwarded to their owners.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-384 requesting copies or loan of selected Japanese Embassy records in Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: The Department requests photostats, microfilm, or a temporary loan of selected records found in the former Japanese Embassy.
subfiles.summary: A preliminary examination indicated that several numbered items in locked safes and filing cabinets merited further study. The Embassy was asked whether the Allied custodians could copy them or lend them to Washington with the understanding that they would be returned after examination.

subfiles.title: Memorandum transmitting translated Belgian personnel and film lists
subfiles.from: C. E. Hammond, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation
subfiles.about: Hammond circulates translations of three French-language lists recovered from the former Japanese Embassy archives in Brussels.
subfiles.summary: The enclosures comprise classifications of neutral, pro-Japanese, and anti-Japanese persons; an inventory of motion-picture films; and a list of persons believed to be Japanese Embassy employees. The documents came from the Brussels archives reported in Despatch No. 219 of June 3, 1946, and were translated in the Department.

subfiles.title: Lists of neutral, pro-Japanese, and anti-Japanese persons in Belgium
subfiles.from: Former Japanese Embassy in Brussels; translated by the Department of State
subfiles.to: Japanese Embassy reference files; later Department of State recipients
subfiles.about: The lists classify Belgian journalists, academics, officials, lawyers, soldiers, businesspeople, and cultural figures by their perceived attitude toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: An opening index labels individuals as neutral, pro-Japanese, or anti-Japanese and records their occupations. Detailed sections then provide addresses, publications, Embassy contacts, travel, lectures, and activities connected with Japan, Manchukuo, or the Sino-Japanese conflict. The records reveal how the Japanese Embassy mapped sympathetic and hostile opinion-makers and tracked personal channels of influence in Belgium.

subfiles.title: List of motion-picture films from the former Japanese Embassy in Brussels
subfiles.from: Former Japanese Embassy in Brussels; translated by the Department of State
subfiles.about: The inventory begins describing 35-mm films concerning Japan, Hirohito’s European tour, Manchuria, and the League of Nations commission.
subfiles.summary: The listed reels include footage of the 1923 Japanese earthquake and fire, Crown Prince Hirohito in Belgium and the Netherlands, and the League of Nations inquiry in Manchuria. Other titles show Harbin, General Honjō at Mukden, Changchun under the name Hsinking, and Japanese industrial investment at Anshan. The inventory continues beyond this section.
